name: Open and Remote if-Conditionals
pattern: Clause with an adjunct PP[if + finite declarative clause]

entry.name: Open and Remote if-Conditionals
entry.pattern: Clause with an adjunct PP[if + finite declarative clause]

1.definition: Sets out a condition and presents a consequence in relation to it.
1.details: The open variant treats the condition as an open possibility. The remote variant characteristically combines a preterite or irrealis form in the condition with a remote modal in the consequence. That preterite can be compatible with an explicitly future time. Present or past remotes often suggest that the condition fails, while a future remote can describe an unsettled possibility.

examples.form: [If he takes the later plane tonight he won’t have to rush.]
examples.note: Open variant with a future time.

examples.form: [If he took the later plane tonight he wouldn’t have to rush.]
examples.note: Remote counterpart. Tonight keeps the condition in the future.

relatedConstructions.notes: The consequent and conditional adjunct are packaged in one construction.
A regular preterite can mark remoteness as well as past time.
A separate use of if introduces an embedded yes/no question.

grounds.note: Catalogues open and more remote condition frames.
Analyzes the open and remote forms and their interpretations.

projection.target: A preterite form in a remote if-clause can describe the same future time as the corresponding present in an open conditional. Remoteness can be marked without asserting that the condition is false.
projection.evidence: CGEL provides matched forms and separates the interpretation from context-dependent implicatures. CASA groups the open and remote variants in three records.

curious.title: If this, then that
curious.summary: An if-phrase sets out a condition, and the rest of the sentence says what follows from it.
curious.body: In If he takes the later plane tonight he won't have to rush, the if-part sets a condition and the rest says what follows. The condition is treated as an open possibility. A second version changes the wording: If he took the later plane tonight he wouldn't have to rush. Both are about tonight, so the changed wording doesn't point to the past. The second marks the possibility as more remote, but that doesn't mean the condition is false.

examples.text: [If he takes the later plane tonight he won't have to rush.]
[If he took the later plane tonight he wouldn't have to rush.]

curious.try: Say a sentence about tomorrow with If and takes. Now say it with took and would. What changes in the feel of it?

teacher.summary: Helps students tell open from remote conditionals, and see that a past form in an if-clause can refer to future time.
teacher.explain: The if-part is an adjunct PP containing a finite declarative clause, and the sentence presents a consequence in relation to it. The open variant treats the condition as an open possibility. The remote variant characteristically combines a preterite or irrealis form in the condition with a remote modal in the consequence. The preterite can be compatible with explicitly future time, as with tonight. Present or past remotes often suggest that the condition fails, while a future remote can describe an unsettled possibility. Remoteness can be marked without asserting that the condition is false. A separate use of if introduces an embedded yes/no question.
teacher.terms: Preterite is the CGEL term for the past tense form. Open and remote are this dictionary's two variants.

examples.text: [If he takes the later plane tonight he won't have to rush.]
[If he took the later plane tonight he wouldn't have to rush.]

contrasts.text: If he takes the later plane tonight he won't have to rush.
contrasts.note: Open variant with a future time.

contrasts.text: If he took the later plane tonight he wouldn't have to rush.
contrasts.note: Remote counterpart. Tonight keeps the condition in the future.

watch_for: A learner might read took in the if-clause as past time, when with tonight it is future.
A learner might assume a remote if-clause says the condition is false.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of open and remote conditionals about plans. They mark the time of each, say what the verb form signals, and rewrite from open to remote.

child.hook: What does if add to a sentence?
child.explain: An if-part names a possibility. The rest says what follows from it. If he takes the later plane tonight, he won't have to rush.

examples.text: [If he takes the later plane tonight he won't have to rush.]
[If he took the later plane tonight he wouldn't have to rush.]

child.play: Say the two example sentences aloud. Which words change? Then make up your own if sentence about tonight, saying the possibility first and then what follows.
